patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2010: Independent Victims' Protection Commission (Klasnic Commission), set up by bishops spring 2010. Set a four-tier compensation model (EUR 5,000 / 15,000 / 25,000 / more in extreme cases)
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Wilhelminenberg children's home, Vienna — commission report; Tyrol and Vorarlberg — state-commissioned study of welfare and residential care (2015); Tyrol — 'Dreierkommission Martinsbühel' report on church-run children's homes (2022); Vienna — historians' commission (2012) and Weisser Ring support programme for victims of city youth welfare (2010–2019).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Bergisch Gladbach abuse complex
cases.who: Chat groups of men sharing recordings of abuse of their own and other children
cases.what: In October 2019 police found a large cache of child abuse images and videos at a house in Bergisch Gladbach; the man there had repeatedly abused his daughter, born in 2017, and shared recordings in chat groups. On 6 October 2020 Cologne Regional Court sentenced him to 12 years plus preventive detention. Investigators found more than 30,000 pseudonyms used in the network, many untraceable; by January 2022 Cologne police had identified 439 suspects, secured numerous convictions and rescued 65 children aged from three months to 17. Two other men, from Krefeld and Viersen, were sentenced to 14.5 and 13.5 years.

cases.title: Elysium darknet platform
cases.who: Elysium (darknet forum and chats, over 87,000 members)
cases.what: Elysium existed from late 2016 and was used to exchange abuse material and to arrange the sexual abuse of children; it had German, French, Spanish and Italian chat groups. German prosecutors (ZIT Frankfurt) and the BKA shut it down in June 2017 after Australian police passed on a lead; 14 suspects were arrested, 12 suspected of abusing children themselves. On 7 March 2019 the Limburg court sentenced four men to between 3 years 10 months and 9 years 9 months, with preventive detention for the main administrator.

cases.title: Austria — Kremsmünster Abbey school abuse, diocesan commission and IPP study
cases.who: Benedictine Abbey of Kremsmünster and its Stiftsgymnasium
cases.what: Abuse at the boarding school of the Benedictine abbey of Kremsmünster in Upper Austria became public in 2010. In July 2013 an Austrian court sentenced a former priest who had been the boarding-school director to 12 years in prison for abusing 24 boys in the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s. A study by the Munich Institute for Practice Research (IPP), commissioned by the abbey and published in March 2015, drew on interviews covering 1945 to 2000 and identified 350 cases of sexual, physical or psychological violence and 24 accused people.

cases.title: Wilhelminenberg children's home, Vienna — commission report
cases.who: City of Vienna children's home at Wilhelminenberg
cases.what: A commission set up by the City of Vienna presented a 344-page report on 12 June 2013, based on 217 interviews including 140 former residents. It found children at the city-run home (1948–1977, girls only from 1962) were rampantly abused, including rape and sexual exploitation by caregivers and outside men, with girls as young as about six. Findings were sent to prosecutors. Some former residents received payments of up to €35,000.
cases.cover_up: Municipal staff in the overseeing department knew of widespread abuse and did not act; city politicians who learned of it in the 1960s also ignored it.

cases.title: Tyrol and Vorarlberg — state-commissioned study of welfare and residential care (2015)
cases.who: State welfare system and residential homes of Tyrol and Vorarlberg, incl. Jagdberg (Schlins), St. Martin (Schwaz), Mariatal (Kramsach), Kleinvolderberg
cases.what: A University of Innsbruck team led by Michaela Ralser, commissioned by the state governments of Tyrol and Vorarlberg, presented its overall study of welfare and residential care on 6 July 2015. It examined four state institutions in detail (Jagdberg, St. Martin, Mariatal and Kleinvolderberg) and found a total institution of isolation and dependence that produced, tolerated and did not prevent physical, psychological and sexualised violence until the 1980s. By then 362 people in Tyrol and 159 in Vorarlberg had received compensation from the states since 2010.
cases.cover_up: The study found the institutional system produced, tolerated and failed to prevent physical, psychological and sexualised violence.

cases.title: Tyrol — 'Dreierkommission Martinsbühel' report on church-run children's homes (2022)
cases.who: Seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol (Martinsbühel, Scharnitz, Josefinum/Volders, Bubenburg/Fügen, St. Josef/Mils, Thurnfeld/Hall, Elisabethinum/Axams); Diocese of Innsbruck; Tyrolean youth welfare
cases.what: A commission set up in 2019 by the State of Tyrol, the Diocese of Innsbruck and religious orders, chaired by Margret Aull, presented its final report 'Demut lernen' on 7 December 2022, written by historians Ina Friedmann and Friedrich Stepanek. Based on 75 interviews, it covered seven church-run children's homes in Tyrol after 1945, where former residents described structural, physical, psychological and sexualised violence; at Martinsbühel in the 1970s one sister looked after up to 50 girls. Survivors said state youth welfare and school authorities did not look closely enough. Bishop Hermann Glettler called the findings 'total pedagogical failure' in church and state institutions, and the state social affairs councillor apologised.
cases.cover_up: Survivors said the state youth welfare office and school authorities looked too little; church and state officials acknowledged institutional responsibility.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Vienna — historians' commission (2012) and Weisser Ring support programme for victims of city youth welfare (2010–2019)
cases.who: City of Vienna youth welfare — municipal, church and private children's homes and foster care, incl. the Kinderübernahmestelle (KÜST)
cases.what: A historians' commission led by Reinhard Sieder reported in May 2012 on Vienna's municipal, church and private children's homes after 1945, through which roughly 100,000 children passed; it described sadistic sexual abuse by some staff alongside widespread violence. The City of Vienna commissioned the victim-support organisation Weisser Ring in 2010 to handle claims of people harmed in Vienna youth welfare institutions between 1945 and 1999. Its final report (2019) records 3,139 reports and financial aid to 2,384 people, with 42.13 million euros paid directly to victims. The separate Wilhelminenberg commission is already on the map.

cases.title: SOS-Kinderdorf Austria — abuse at Imst and Moosburg, founder Hermann Gmeiner, and the Griss reform commission (2025–2026)
cases.who: SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich — children's villages incl. Imst (Tyrol) and Moosburg (Carinthia); founder Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986)
cases.what: After a Falter report in September 2025 on abuse by staff at Austrian SOS children's villages, SOS-Kinderdorf Österreich said on 23 October 2025 that there were credible allegations that its founder Hermann Gmeiner (died 1986) sexually and physically abused eight boys at four villages between the 1950s and 1980s; victims had come forward from 2013 and received compensation and therapy, but the organisation had not made this public. A later investigation report listed 16 suspected cases of sexualised violence by Gmeiner. An external reform commission chaired by former Supreme Court president Irmgard Griss presented its results on 25 June 2026, focusing on abuse at Moosburg and Imst, handling of earlier studies and possible cover-ups, and the lack of external oversight. Prosecutors in Klagenfurt, Innsbruck and Salzburg opened investigations.
cases.cover_up: The allegations against Gmeiner were known internally for years (victims came forward 2013–2023) but were made public only in 2025.

cases.title: Cardinal Groër affair and Klasnic victims' commission, Austria
cases.who: Archdiocese of Vienna; Austrian Bishops' Conference; Independent Victims' Protection Commission (Klasnic Commission)
cases.what: Archbishop of Vienna Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër stepped down in September 1995 after a former pupil, followed by others, accused him of sexual abuse; in 1998 Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded, and the Holy See opened an inquiry. In spring 2010 the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission chaired by Waltraud Klasnic. By 31 August 2021, according to the church's victims' foundation, payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total. At Kremsmünster Abbey, the former head of the boarding school was jailed for 12 years in 2013 for crimes against 24 former pupils, 15 of them victims of sexual abuse.

cases.title: New Zealand DIA-led operation: 146 children safeguarded
cases.who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
cases.what: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. By March 2022 it had opened 836 cases internationally, led to 46 arrests across New Zealand, identified more than 100 suspects in the EU and safeguarded 146 children; in Austria and Hungary suspects were abusing their own children.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Austria-led 2007 investigation — 2,360 suspects in 77 countries
cases.who: Online distribution network uncovered by Austrian authorities
cases.what: The investigation began in July 2006 when an employee of a Vienna-based file-hosting service reported suspicious material; within 24 hours investigators recorded more than 8,000 hits from 2,361 IP addresses in 77 countries. On 7 February 2007 Austrian authorities announced more than 2,360 suspects who had paid to view videos of young children being sexually abused; the FBI was investigating about 600, about 130 were Australian, France was looking at about 100 and at least 23 were Austrian. Germany had the largest number of suspects. No suspects were yet in custody at the announcement.
cases.cover_up: The two Irish suspects were not investigated by the Garda until six months after Austria notified them.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

cases.title: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.

networks.what: Darknet forum with over 87,000 members used to share material and arrange abuse; four operators convicted 2019.

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: North Rhine-Westphalia abuse complexes (Lügde, Bergisch Gladbach)
networks.what: Linked series of investigations into men abusing children and sharing recordings in chat groups; Bergisch Gladbach alone produced 439 suspects. Münster complex (2020) not documented here — page not retrieved.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 5,456 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: 2000: Brazil: 2000 law punishing subjecting a child or adolescent to prostitution with 4-10 years
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: Largest Catholic population in the world; cases surfaced through individual prosecutions and a 2010 parliamentary hearing on one priest
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Brazil — three Arapiraca priests convicted (Penedo diocese)
cases.who: Diocese of Penedo
cases.what: On 19 December 2011 a juvenile court judge in Arapiraca convicted Monsignor Luiz Marques Barbosa (21 years), Monsignor Raimundo Gomes and Fr Edílson Duarte (16 years 4 months each) of abusing altar boys. The case began with complaints from former altar boys in March 2010 and a secretly filmed video broadcast on SBT television.
cases.cover_up: According to the victims, Bishop Valério Breda knew what was happening; he suspended the priests two days after the scandal broke. The convicted priests were not jailed pending appeal.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Brazil — Joint Congressional Inquiry (CPMI) into networks sexually exploiting children (2004)
cases.who: Networks including politicians, businessmen and clergy named by the commission
cases.what: A joint commission of 11 senators and 11 deputies, created in 2003 to investigate violence and networks of sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, had by May 2004 received more than 800 complaints, heard more than 300 people and visited 14 states. Its final report, approved on 13 July 2004, put more than 250 people on notice, among them 20 serving politicians (including one federal deputy, two state deputies and three mayors), about 30 businessmen and five priests, and passed the cases to federal and state prosecutors. The commission's bill rewriting the Penal Code chapter on 'crimes against public morals' (PLS 253/2004) became Law 12.015 of 2009.

cases.title: Brazil — Senate 'CPI da Pedofilia' on online abuse material and child abuse (2008–2010)
cases.who: Users of the Orkut social network and offenders across Brazil; the CPI's hearings were credited with the fall of a Pará state deputy, Luiz Afonso Sefer, convicted at first instance in 2010
cases.what: The Federal Senate's parliamentary inquiry into paedophilia, chaired by Senator Magno Malta, worked for almost three years, the longest CPI to date, and its rapporteur Demóstenes Torres handed a final report of nearly 1,700 pages to police and prosecutors in December 2010. It signed a conduct agreement with Google, the Federal Police and prosecutors to lift secrecy on Orkut pages linked to child sexual abuse. Rádio Senado reported that hundreds of people were arrested or indicted after its work, and Malta credited the CPI's hearings with the fall of Belém state deputy Luiz Afonso Sefer; Sefer was convicted in 2010 of raping a child, but the case has since been overturned, reinstated and annulled on appeal and, as of February 2026, his 20-year sentence had not been carried out. Laws passed during its work criminalised possession of child abuse material and ordered the closure of businesses where children were exploited.

cases.title: Brazil — Chamber of Deputies inquiry asks indictment of 37, including a mayor and state deputies (2014)
cases.who: Local politicians and others in Amazonas, Minas Gerais and other states
cases.what: A parliamentary inquiry of the Chamber of Deputies, installed in 2012 with Deputy Liliam Sá as rapporteur, approved its final report on 4 June 2014. It asked for the indictment of 37 people for sexual exploitation of children and adolescents, among them the mayor of Coari (Amazonas), Adail Pinheiro, a serving Amazonas state deputy, a former state deputy and a former president of the Três Corações city council.

cases.title: Brazil — Federal Highway Police 'Projeto Mapear' of child sexual exploitation points on highways
cases.who: Truck stops, bars, motels along federal highways
cases.what: Brazil's Federal Highway Police (PRF) and Childhood Brasil have mapped roadside sites vulnerable to child sexual exploitation for about 19 years. The 2021–2022 survey, released 31 May 2023, assessed more than 9,700 points, rating 640 critical and about 1,800 high-risk; the worst conditions were on BR-116 (12 critical points), BR-153, BR-101, BR-163, BR-232 and BR-040. An earlier edition found 69% of victims female and 22% transgender, and 38% from elsewhere, possibly trafficked. The 2025 US TIP report says child sex trafficking is common along BR-386, BR-116 and BR-255.

cases.title: Operation Lobos / Baby Heart (Brazil-led)
cases.who: Baby Heart and other Tor boards
cases.what: A year-long global investigation into the Tor child-abuse site 'Babyheart' and its administrator involved the UK NCA and West Midlands Police, Australian Federal Police and Queensland's Task Force Argos, Toronto Police, the Brazilian Federal Police, INTERPOL, Europol and US ICE, with nine countries listed (Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Italy, Portugal, the US and the UK). Intelligence narrowed the administrator's location to Portugal, where the Portuguese Judicial Police arrested and charged him in 2017; examination of his devices identified seven victims directly related to him. INTERPOL and Portuguese police presented the case publicly on 23 January 2020. Brazil's Federal Police ran related 'Operação Lobos' phases.

cases.title: Brazil orders Discord to suspend livestreaming (2026)
cases.who: Discord Inc.
cases.what: On 12 August 2026 Brazil's National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) ordered Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature nationwide, saying it had found 'robust evidence' that Discord failed to take reasonable steps to stop minors being exposed to content promoting violence, self-harm and suicide. The order followed the death in July 2026 of a 13-year-old girl in central-western Brazil who, authorities said, was encouraged during a Discord livestream to take her own life. Five teenagers were arrested in connection with her death, and police said the investigation also led them to another girl at risk, whom they reached in time. A Justice Ministry cyber-intelligence official called the case 'a terrible failure in moderation'.

cases.title: Brazil — child sex tourism in northeastern coastal cities (Fortaleza, Natal, Recife, Salvador)
cases.who: Taxi drivers, hotel and bar staff facilitating foreign offenders
cases.what: In 2006 Brazil's Federal Police described sex tourism as most frequent in Fortaleza, Recife, Salvador and Natal, and ran periodic raids, e.g. on a Ponta Negra (Natal) nightclub with 110 foreigners (no children found that night). The 2025 US TIP report says taxi drivers and hotel, bar and nightclub staff in coastal tourist destinations facilitate child sex trafficking, and cites a study suggesting up to 16 per cent of girls aged 14–17 in one northeastern metropolitan area were likely victims of commercial sexual exploitation.
cases.cover_up: US TIP 2025: no investigations of complicit officials reported; a 2016 child sex-trafficking case involving an elected official in Paraná unresolved.

In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions); China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: Almost no reports reach the international systems
patterns.role_note: NCMEC 2025: 9,406 reports for China (population ~1.4bn) versus 1,933,900 for India — US platforms are largely blocked in China, so CyberTipline data is blind there
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions)
cases.who: Six state orphanages in Hunan; traffickers from Guangdong; local officials
cases.what: Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. In 2005, according to Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired; three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to 3–13 years.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: Myanmar → China — Kachin women and girls sold as 'brides' (HRW 2019)
cases.who: Traffickers including relatives and acquaintances; buying families in China
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's 112-page report of 21 March 2019 documented women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States, many displaced by conflict, sold for US$3,000–13,000 to Chinese families, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. One survivor was trafficked at 16 by her sister-in-law. The 2025 US TIP report says displaced women and girls in Kachin and Shan remain vulnerable to forced marriage and forced childbearing in China.
cases.cover_up: HRW said Myanmar and Chinese authorities were 'looking away'; police on both sides gave traffickers little reason to fear enforcement.

cases.title: Vietnam and Laos → China — girls sold as brides (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers and marriage brokers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP reports say traffickers in Vietnamese border villages lure women and girls, particularly Hmong, to China for forced marriages involving sex trafficking or forced labour, and use 'bride kidnapping' to exploit ethnic-minority girls in the northwest highlands; in Laos, traffickers increasingly kidnap or recruit women and girls via marriage brokers to China for sex trafficking, forced labour and forced surrogacy. Vietnam identified 236 child victims in 2024.

cases.title: Mongolia — girls sex-trafficked in Ulaanbaatar hotels and karaoke bars (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers in hotels, massage parlours, karaoke clubs
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says women and girls are sex-trafficked in Mongolian hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in Ulaanbaatar, provincial centres and border areas, sometimes facilitated by a lack of police enforcement; traffickers use online platforms to groom and blackmail children; and children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, e.g. as horse jockeys.
cases.cover_up: The report says exploitation is sometimes facilitated by lack of police enforcement; some families are complicit.

cases.title: Pakistan → China — 629 girls and women sold as 'brides' (AP 2019)
cases.who: Brokers selling poor (often Christian) Pakistani girls and women to Chinese men
cases.what: AP obtained a list compiled by Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency of 629 girls and women sold as brides to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019. In October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals charged in the biggest case. The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers target impoverished Christian communities to send women and girls to China, where hundreds reported being forced into commercial sex.
cases.cover_up: Officials told AP the investigation largely stopped after June 2019 because of pressure from government officials fearful of harming ties with Beijing; in October 2019 a Faisalabad court acquitted 31 Chinese nationals after witnesses were threatened or bribed into silence.

flows.title: China → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from China, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 7,906 in FY2005).

flows.title: China → United States
flows.what: China sent about 160,000 children abroad for adoption from 1992 until it ended the programme on 5 September 2024; others went to Spain, Canada, the UK, the Netherlands, France and Australia.

flows.title: Pakistan → China ('bride' trafficking)
flows.what: Brokers sold poor Pakistani girls and women, many Christian, to Chinese men as brides.

flows.title: Kachin State, Myanmar → Yunnan and beyond, China ('bride' trafficking)
flows.what: Women and girls sold for $3,000–13,000 to Chinese families.

flows.title: Northern Vietnam → China (forced marriage)
flows.what: Hmong and other ethnic-minority women and girls lured or abducted to China for forced marriage.

flows.title: Laos → China (forced marriage, surrogacy)
flows.what: Lao women and girls kidnapped or recruited via marriage brokers to China.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Germany → South Africa: Fr Georg Kerkhoff (extradited back); Germany → South America: Jesuit Fr Wolfgang S.; Essen → Munich: Fr Peter Hullermann.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Odenwaldschule: first report 1998, first action 2010 (12 years). Victims came forward 1998 and Frankfurter Rundschau reported Nov 1999; promised review never took place; prosecutors dropped the case as time-barred Lügde campsite: first report 2016, first action 2019 (3 years). Police received two tips in 2016; youth office placed a foster child with the main offender; 155 evidence items vanished from a police office Peter Hullermann (Munich): first report 1979, first action 1986 (7 years). Accepted into Munich in 1980 under Cardinal Ratzinger for therapy and given pastoral work, abused again
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: 2013: Bundestag (March 2013) extended civil limitation for sexual abuse claims from 3 to 30 years (s.197 BGB); criminal limitation starts running only at victim's 21st birthday (s.78b StGB). Not retroactive for already time-barred claims
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2010: Round Table on Sexual Child Abuse (Runder Tisch), federal government, 24 Mar 2010 - final report 30 Nov 2011; Independent Commissioner (UBSKM) from 2010. Set up after the January 2010 Canisius-Kolleg revelations; chaired by three federal ministers
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Paul Schäfer / Colonia Dignidad (2019): Hopp living in Germany; investigation dropped
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.role_note: 2 documented adoption flows into Germany on this map.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 1993: Germany: extraterritorial jurisdiction for sexual abuse of children abroad (s.5 no.8 StGB), even where the act is legal at the place of the offence
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Proven link to a state service
patterns.role_note: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad (proven link to a state service). 'Kentler experiment' — Berlin youth office placed children with paedophile foster fathers (proven link to a state service).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 18,401 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (6% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.role_note: 'Kentler experiment' — Berlin youth office placed children with paedophile foster fathers; Lügde campsite abuse — youth office placed foster child with offender; Sebastian Edathy (Bundestag) — images of naked minors; case closed on payment; Archdiocese of Hamburg — University of Ulm study of abuse in Mecklenburg 1946–1989 (2023); Independent Commission (UKASK) study of paedosexual networks in Berlin (2021); Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Bergisch Gladbach abuse complex
cases.who: Chat groups of men sharing recordings of abuse of their own and other children
cases.what: In October 2019 police found a large cache of child abuse images and videos at a house in Bergisch Gladbach; the man there had repeatedly abused his daughter, born in 2017, and shared recordings in chat groups. On 6 October 2020 Cologne Regional Court sentenced him to 12 years plus preventive detention. Investigators found more than 30,000 pseudonyms used in the network, many untraceable; by January 2022 Cologne police had identified 439 suspects, secured numerous convictions and rescued 65 children aged from three months to 17. Two other men, from Krefeld and Viersen, were sentenced to 14.5 and 13.5 years.

cases.title: Lügde campsite abuse — youth office placed foster child with offender
cases.who: Two men at a permanent campsite; youth welfare offices of Lippe and Hameln-Pyrmont; Lippe police
cases.what: On 5 September 2019 the Detmold regional court sentenced Andreas V. to 13 years and Mario S. to 12 years, both followed by preventive detention, for abusing 32 children at a campsite in Lügde from 1998 to 2018; police found 32,000 files of abuse material. Youth welfare authorities had placed a foster daughter with Andreas V. The North Rhine-Westphalia Landtag inquiry (interim report 24 March 2022) found failures by police and the youth offices of Lippe and Hameln-Pyrmont.
cases.cover_up: Welfare authorities placed a foster girl with the main offender despite allegations about him. Police failed to act on repeated complaints, evidence disappeared from police archives, and a case worker manipulated and deleted files. The NRW parliamentary inquiry found 'authority failure' and said the men could have been stopped two years earlier.

cases.title: Elysium darknet platform
cases.who: Elysium (darknet forum and chats, over 87,000 members)
cases.what: Elysium existed from late 2016 and was used to exchange abuse material and to arrange the sexual abuse of children; it had German, French, Spanish and Italian chat groups. German prosecutors (ZIT Frankfurt) and the BKA shut it down in June 2017 after Australian police passed on a lead; 14 suspects were arrested, 12 suspected of abusing children themselves. On 7 March 2019 the Limburg court sentenced four men to between 3 years 10 months and 9 years 9 months, with preventive detention for the main administrator.

cases.title: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site
cases.who: Colonia Dignidad sect led by Paul Schäfer; Chile's secret police DINA; West German embassy
cases.what: Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal wanted in Germany on child abuse charges, founded the Colonia Dignidad commune in southern Chile in 1961. Chilean officials believe the colony was used as a centre for torture of opponents of the Pinochet dictatorship between 1973 and 1990, and Schäfer was charged with aiding the regime. The colony recruited children from local farms into its free school and clinic; an investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer fled to Argentina, was arrested there in March 2005 and returned to Chile, and on 24–25 May 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children; with further convictions for torture, weapons and a murder his sentences totalled 33 years. He died in prison in 2010. The colony's doctor, Hartmut Hopp, was convicted in Chile in 2011 of 16 counts of aiding child sexual abuse.
cases.cover_up: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them. Schäfer fled in 1997 and was caught in Argentina in March 2005.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
cases.who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
cases.what: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.

cases.title: Peter Hullermann — transferred from Essen to Munich 1980
cases.who: Archdiocese of Munich and Freising; Diocese of Essen
cases.what: In January 1980 the Munich archdiocese under Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger agreed to receive Fr Peter Hullermann from the Diocese of Essen for therapy after he had been suspended there over abuse of a boy. He was then given pastoral work, abused minors again, and in June 1986 was convicted, fined 4,000 marks and given an 18-month suspended sentence with five years' probation. He kept serving in Bavarian parishes until the archdiocese suspended him in March 2010. Then vicar general Gerhard Gruber took 'full responsibility' for letting him back into pastoral work.
cases.cover_up: Accused priest accepted into Munich for therapy in January 1980 with Cardinal Ratzinger's approval, then reassigned to pastoral work where he abused again; remained a priest until 2010

cases.title: Diocese of Passau — University of Passau study (2025)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Passau — priests, deacons and religious brothers
cases.what: A University of Passau team led by historian Marc von Knorring, commissioned by the diocese's independent review commission, published its study online on 8 December 2025 covering 1945 to 2022. It found at least 672 minors, mostly boys, who were sexually abused or physically mistreated (or both) by 154 clergy, about 6.4% of some 2,400 priests, deacons and religious clergy in the period; 128 of them sexually abused minors, and about 86% were likely repeat offenders. Abuse took place in boarding schools and homes, religious lessons and altar-server duties. The study found bishops and vicars general often protected the institution and the priesthood rather than victims.
cases.cover_up: Bishops and vicars general often put protecting the institution and the priesthood above victims; judges, prosecutors, medical experts and school and youth authorities are named as bystanders.

cases.title: Germany — Diocese of Münster, University of Münster study (2022)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Münster
cases.what: Historians at the University of Münster, including Thomas Großbölting, published a study of the diocese on 13 June 2022 after about two and a half years of research. It found at least 610 minors abused by 196 clerics between 1945 and 2020, about 4% of the diocese's priests in that period, and estimated the real number of victims at 8 to 10 times higher. Bishops and diocesan leaders were often fully informed, covered up cases or intervened only superficially, and usually transferred accused priests.
cases.cover_up: The study found a 'massive leadership failure' under the bishops from 1947 to 2008; most accused priests were transferred rather than restricted.

flows.title: Seoul → Germany
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Germany; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Colombo → Germany
flows.what: Sri Lankan children adopted to Germany in the 1980s (baby-farm period).

flows.title: Occupied Poland → Germany (removal)
flows.what: Polish children kidnapped for Germanization and placed with German families via Lebensborn/RuSHA.

flows.what: Berlin youth authorities placed children with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, including outside Berlin; the Hildesheim report names Hannover and other Lower Saxony locations as network nodes.

flows.what: Schäfer fled abuse accusations in Germany in 1961 and the colony kept 'importing' children.

flows.what: 6% of IWF-actioned URLs in 2025.

flows.what: Operation Stream intelligence went to 38 countries; Wikipedia reports 30 arrests in the UK from 60 identified.

flows.title: Boystown administrator arrested in Paraguay
flows.what: One of Boystown's German administrators was living in Paraguay and arrested there in April 2021.

flows.title: Romania → Western Europe (sex trafficking of women and girls)
flows.what: Most identified Romanian victims are women and girls exploited in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK.

flows.title: Germany → South Africa: Fr Georg Kerkhoff (extradited back)
flows.what: A German priest with abuse cases pending at home worked for years in South Africa, where he was tried for abusing boys at a 2008 camp, then extradited and jailed in Krefeld in 2015.

networks.name: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.
networks.what: RuSHA racially screened children in occupied territories and Lebensborn ran camps and homes from which selected children were placed with German families under new identities. The Nuremberg RuSHA trial (1947–48) ruled the kidnapping and Germanization of children part of genocide.

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Kentler network (West German youth welfare and pedagogy)
networks.what: A network of academics, youth welfare officials and educators around sexologist Helmut Kentler who supported, legitimised or tolerated paedophile positions. Berlin youth authorities placed children with paedophile foster fathers from the late 1960s into the 2000s.

networks.name: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
networks.what: National Scout associations; the Boy Scouts of America faced more than 82,000 sexual abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy and had kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers.

networks.name: Colonia Dignidad / Villa Baviera
networks.what: German sect enclave in Chile led by Paul Schäfer, convicted in 2006 of abusing 25 minors. Used by Pinochet's secret police DINA as a detention and torture site (Rettig Commission 1991). Germany's president acknowledged diplomatic failures in 2016.

networks.name: Welcome to Video
networks.what: Darknet video site paid in Bitcoin, about 1.2 million members; seized 2018. 337 arrests in 38 countries announced October 2019. Start year 2015 is not in the sources opened and is omitted from cases.

networks.name: Dreamboard
networks.what: Invitation-only board, about 600 members; 72 charged in Operation Delego (2011). Start year is approximate (investigation launched 2009).

networks.name: Elysium
networks.what: Darknet forum with over 87,000 members used to share material and arrange abuse; four operators convicted 2019.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2011: Finland — SRK (Conservative Laestadian) internal report.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

cases.title: Finland — maltreatment in child welfare substitute care 1937–1983
cases.who: Finnish child welfare institutions and foster care
cases.what: A Ministry of Social Affairs and Health study interviewed about 300 people who had been in child welfare substitute care between 1937 and 1983 and found maltreatment and violence in all forms of care. The Finnish government made an official apology on 20 November 2016, Universal Children's Day.

cases.title: Finland — Conservative Laestadian movement (SRK) admits 70–100 child abuse cases mishandled
cases.who: Central Committee of Conservative Laestadian Congregations (SRK), Finland's largest revivalist movement within the Lutheran church
cases.what: In April 2011 the SRK, which has about 35,000 members, announced that an internal report had found 70 to 100 cases of child sexual abuse within the movement since the 1980s. Most involved abuse within member families rather than by church officials, but the SRK admitted its officials had mishandled the cases and lacked the knowledge to respond. A study by Johanna Hurtig (University of Tampere) on abuse in the movement was published the same year.
cases.cover_up: SRK admitted officials 'mishandled' cases, did not use expert help and did not communicate, which could look like downplaying or covering up.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.
