patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 24,212 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2007: scandal + law: Casa Quivira raid (August, 46 children); Hague-compliant adoption law passed 11 December 2007 2008: closure: Guatemala stops new adoptions to the US from 1 January; US State Dept (9 January) says no new US adoptions until Hague-compliant 2010: report: CICIG report on illegal adoption finds 78% of 153 cases studied violated the law
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007); Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls; Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls
cases.who: State-run children's home under the Secretariat of Social Welfare (SBS); National Civil Police
cases.what: About 700 children lived at the state home, built for a maximum of 500; most had committed no crime. Months before the fire prosecutors had recommended closing it over abuse allegations, and girls had protested overcrowding and alleged sexual abuse by staff. After an escape on 7 March 2017, police returned a group of girls and locked them in a room; on 8 March one girl set a mattress alight, killing 41 girls and injuring 15. The social welfare secretary, his deputy and the home's director were sacked and later charged. On 12 Aug 2025 a judge convicted six former officials of offences from manslaughter to abuse of authority, with sentences of 6 to 25 years; former secretary Carlos Rodas received 25 years and a police officer who held the key 13 years. The judge said the fire was the culmination of reported abuses not acted on, and ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales.
cases.cover_up: Officials ignored repeated complaints: in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for precautionary measures citing mistreatment and a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On the day of the fire police guarding the locked room did not let the girls out.

cases.title: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
cases.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
cases.what: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

cases.title: Rendon-Reyes trafficking organization (Tenancingo)
cases.who: Rendon-Reyes Trafficking Organization, Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
cases.what: From December 2004 to November 2015 the Tenancingo-based Rendon-Reyes organization smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the US, forced them into prostitution and laundered proceeds back to Mexico. In January 2019 five members were sentenced in Brooklyn to between 15 and 25 years; others had pleaded guilty to racketeering and sex trafficking.

cases.title: Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989)
cases.who: Guatemalan armed forces and National Police; Secretaría de Bienestar Social (Hogar Elisa Martínez); notaries and courts
cases.what: In September 2009 the Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, part of the Peace Secretariat of the Presidency set up under President Álvaro Colom, published a study of adoptions during the internal armed conflict. It reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files recorded for 1977–1989 and found that the army and National Police transported children into the adoption system, that adoptions often rested on court declarations of abandonment with little effort to find parents, and that a 1977 decree let notaries formalise adoptions without a judge. Chief investigator Marco Tulio Álvarez told the press the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France.
cases.cover_up: Decree 54-77 (1977) let notaries complete adoptions without prior judicial approval; the welfare secretariat kept no record of how many children it received

cases.title: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007)
cases.who: Private notaries (notarios), baby brokers, foster homes, officials
cases.what: After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way. Guatemala passed a Hague-compliant law on 11 December 2007 and stopped new adoptions to the US from 1 January 2008; the US State Department announced on 9 January 2008 it would not allow new adoptions until procedures were compliant.

cases.title: Lev Tahor — Guatemala removal of 160 minors
cases.who: Lev Tahor
cases.what: In December 2024 Guatemalan authorities removed 160 minors from a Lev Tahor farm compound in Oratorio after abuse and trafficking complaints; in January 2025 Interpol arrested a member in Guatemala on trafficking charges. The group had earlier fled child-protection proceedings in Quebec (2013, where authorities sought care for 127 children) and Ontario.

cases.title: Guatemala — Casa Quivira raid: 46 children possibly stolen for adoption
cases.who: Casa Quivira private adoption home (run by a US citizen and his Guatemalan wife); two lawyers
cases.what: On 11 August 2007 Guatemalan police found 46 children aged a few days to three years at the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children daily. Two lawyers who allegedly processed the adoptions were arrested. Attorney General Mario Gordillo said most of the children lacked proper documents and his office was investigating whether they had been stolen or obtained from mothers under coercion.

cases.title: Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala — gangs exploit girls; North American offenders (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Gangs and criminal organizations; foreign offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP reports say criminal organizations including gangs exploit girls in sex trafficking in urban Honduras and Guatemala, and that men from Canada and the US exploit Honduran children. In El Salvador, foreign tourists sexually exploit children and the rapid growth of tourism has created new risks; an estimated 140,000–200,000 Salvadoran children have a parent abroad or detained. Guatemalan children are exploited in Mexico and the US and in live-streamed abuse.

flows.title: Guatemala City → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Guatemala, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 4,728 in FY2007).

flows.title: Guatemala / Honduras → Mexico → United States (children in sex trafficking)
flows.what: Guatemalan and Honduran adults and children exploited in sex trafficking in Mexico, the US, Belize and El Salvador.

flows.title: Chatham-Kent, Ontario → Guatemala (Lev Tahor flees child-protection orders)
flows.what: After a Quebec court ordered 14 children into foster care in November 2013 and the group moved to Ontario, members with children left for Guatemala in 2014; nine who tried to flee via Trinidad and Tobago were returned to Canada.

networks.name: Tenancingo (Tlaxcala) pimping family networks
networks.what: Family-based pimping networks from Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, that recruited Mexican and Central American women and girls by deception and forced them into prostitution in New York and other US cities. Several were prosecuted in Brooklyn (Carreto family, 2005–2008; Rendon-Reyes organization, 2019).

networks.name: Lev Tahor
networks.what: Ultra-Orthodox sect of about 200–300 people founded in Israel in 1988 by Shlomo Helbrans, accused of child abuse and forced marriage of teenage girls. Leaders were convicted in the US in 2021 of kidnapping two children.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: 2000: Statute of Limitations (Amendment) Act 2000 (passed 21 June 2000) gave a one-year window to bring claims for sexual abuse suffered as a minor and introduced a disability-based extension
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Holy See and the Murphy Commission (Ireland): No Vatican files supplied
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State-backed adoption systems that falsified children's papers
patterns.role_note: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad.
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2017: Ireland: Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 2017 gives worldwide jurisdiction over Irish offenders
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad; Ryan Commission — state-funded industrial schools and reformatories, Ireland; Mother and Baby Homes Commission — Ireland; Ireland — illegal birth registrations: St Patrick's Guild (126 cases) and the 2021 sampling review; Ferns Report — Diocese of Ferns; Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin; Ryan Commission — industrial schools run by religious orders.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
cases.who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
cases.what: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.
cases.cover_up: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994

cases.title: Diocese of Raphoe — Fr Eugene Greene
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Raphoe
cases.what: Fr Eugene Greene, the most notorious offender in the Diocese of Raphoe, was sentenced in 1999 to 12 years in prison for abusing 26 boys over 20 years. A church safeguarding review published on 30 November 2011 found allegations against 14 Raphoe priests between 1975 and 2010, four of whom had been convicted, and pointed to 'significant errors of judgement' by successive bishops. Former bishop Séamus Hegarty said his past practice was 'sometimes poor' and apologised.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Freedom Hosting — Tor host for Lolita City and other abuse sites
cases.who: Freedom Hosting (Eric Eoin Marques, convicted)
cases.what: Freedom Hosting was a free anonymous dark web hosting service that ran from July 2008 to July 2013 and hosted over 200 child exploitation websites, including Lolita City, which Anonymous had attacked in 2011. The operator, Eric Eoin Marques, was arrested in Dublin in early August 2013 on a US warrant; the FBI accused him of being 'the largest facilitator of child porn on the planet'. After Ireland's Supreme Court dismissed his challenge in March 2019 he was extradited, pleaded guilty on 6 February 2020 to conspiracy to advertise child sexual abuse material, and on 16 September 2021 was sentenced to 27 years. DOJ said the sites held millions of images and videos, over 1.97 million not previously known to law enforcement.
cases.cover_up: Extradition from Ireland took from 2013 to 2019 through appeals.

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady
cases.who: Diocese of Stockton; Bishop Roger Mahony (later Cardinal Archbishop of Los Angeles)
cases.what: Irish-born priest Oliver O'Grady, ordained in 1971 for the Diocese of Stockton, abused children from about 1973 and was moved between parishes. Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns by 1980 and moved him in 1984. O'Grady was convicted in 1993 and sentenced to 14 years; a 1998 civil jury awarded $30 million (reduced to $7 million). Paroled and deported to Ireland in 2000, he was convicted there for child abuse images in 2012 and 2020.
cases.cover_up: After police declined to charge him in 1984, Bishop Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor; Mahony said he was unaware of molestation reports, although a letter about earlier abuse was in O'Grady's personnel file.

cases.title: Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin
cases.what: The Commission of Investigation into the Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin reported on 26 November 2009. It examined a representative sample of 46 priests out of 102 within its remit; 320 people complained of child sexual abuse between 1975 and 2004. It found former Archbishops McQuaid, Ryan, McNamara and Connell failed to report what they knew to the Gardaí, and said the archdiocese's move to take out insurance against abuse claims showed it knew abuse was a potential major cost. It also criticised the Gardaí for treating priests as outside their remit; the Garda Commissioner called the report 'difficult and disturbing reading'.
cases.cover_up: Abuse 'covered up' 1975–2004; bishops generally did not report to Gardaí before 1996; archdiocese took out insurance against abuse litigation from 1987; Gardaí knew of complaints against Fr Tony Walsh in 1990–91 and took no action

cases.title: Ireland — illegal birth registrations: St Patrick's Guild (126 cases) and the 2021 sampling review
cases.who: St Patrick's Guild adoption society; Tusla and the Adoption Authority of Ireland (record holders); the Irish state
cases.what: In May 2018 the Irish government announced that 126 people placed through the St Patrick's Guild adoption society had been illegally registered as the birth children of their adoptive parents. An independent review then sampled 1,496 of about 150,000 adoption records; its report, published in March 2021, found about 265 files with suspicious markers and estimated 5,540 to 19,980 files might show similar signs. Tusla reported evidence of coerced consent, children placed abroad with little documentation and altered names and birth dates; the report did not recommend a full file review.

cases.title: Ireland — Murphy inquiry into child sexual abuse in swimming (1998)
cases.who: Irish Amateur Swimming Association (IASA); national coaches including Derry O'Rourke and George Gibney (Gibney never tried)
cases.what: The Irish government asked senior counsel Roderick Murphy to inquire after former Olympic coach Derry O'Rourke was jailed for 12 years for abusing 11 girl swimmers. His 165-page report (1998) found that children had come to believe abuse was a normal part of their training, and a 'total systems failure' in the Irish Amateur Swimming Association. It noted Garda investigations into two other coaches and made more than 100 recommendations; the minister cut the association's funding.
cases.cover_up: The report found 'total systems failure' in the IASA; charges against another coach were dropped after a 1994 judicial review because of delay.

cases.title: Madonna House residential centre, Dublin — Department of Health inquiry (1996)
cases.who: Madonna House children's residential centre, run by the Sisters of Charity
cases.what: The report of the inquiry into Madonna House, a Sisters of Charity residential centre for children in Dublin, was published in 1996 with its most damaging sections removed on legal advice. The withheld sections, revealed in May 1999 after RTÉ's States of Fear team obtained them, described beatings, humiliation and sexual assaults on children by a small number of staff, and management that failed to take effective action on staff concerns and children's complaints.
cases.cover_up: Management failed to act on staff concerns and children's complaints; one staff member regarded as having an inappropriate relationship with a girl was paid to live elsewhere but kept his job; the sections describing abuse were removed from the published 1996 report and only revealed in 1999.

cases.title: Ferns Report — Diocese of Ferns
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Ferns
cases.what: The state Ferns Inquiry, published 25 October 2005, examined more than 100 allegations of child sexual abuse made between 1962 and 2002 against 21 priests of the diocese. Bishop Donal Herlihy moved accused priests temporarily and then reinstated them, and ordained men he knew or should have known posed a risk. Bishop Brendan Comiskey never got a priest to stand aside from ministry. The report found Garda handling of one of eight formal complaints 'wholly inadequate' and some pre-1988 complaints were not recorded.
cases.cover_up: Bishop Herlihy moved accused priests to other posts or dioceses for a period, then reinstated them; Gardaí failed to record or properly investigate some pre-1988 complaints

cases.title: Cloyne Report — Diocese of Cloyne
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Cloyne; Bishop John Magee
cases.what: The Cloyne Report, published 13 July 2011, examined the diocese's handling of allegations against 19 clerics from 1996 to February 2009, after the Irish church had adopted reporting procedures. Nine complaints that should have been reported to the Gardaí were not, and none were reported to the health authorities. Bishop John Magee was found to have shown little interest in applying the guidelines for 12 years. The report said the Vatican's response to the Irish procedures allowed bishops to ignore them.
cases.cover_up: Nine complaints that should have gone to the Gardaí were not reported; none of the 1996–2008 complaints reported to the health service; Vatican's reaction to Irish guidelines described as 'entirely unhelpful'

cases.title: Ryan Commission — industrial schools run by religious orders
cases.who: Christian Brothers (most boys' institutions), Sisters of Mercy (most girls' institutions) and other Catholic orders
cases.what: The Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse reported on 20 May 2009 after a nine-year investigation of more than 250 church-run institutions that held over 30,000 children from the 1930s to the 1990s. It found sexual abuse 'endemic' in boys' institutions run mainly by the Christian Brothers; the Sisters of Mercy ran most girls' institutions. The 2,600-page report names no perpetrators after a Christian Brothers lawsuit. A parallel state redress scheme paid about 12,000 people an average of €65,000.
cases.cover_up: Christian Brothers sued the commission in 2004 to keep members' names out; no real names of perpetrators published; findings not to be used for prosecutions; state Department of Education inspections failed

cases.title: Scoping Inquiry — abuse in religious-run schools
cases.who: 42 religious orders that ran day and boarding schools
cases.what: The state Scoping Inquiry, published 3 September 2024, recorded 2,395 allegations of sexual abuse against 884 alleged abusers at 308 schools run by 42 religious orders, mostly from the 1960s to the 1990s. 590 allegations involving 190 alleged abusers concerned 17 special schools. More than half of the alleged abusers are dead. The government announced a full Commission of Investigation.

cases.title: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad
cases.who: Religious orders (incl. Bon Secours Sisters), local authorities and the Irish state
cases.what: The Commission of Investigation's final report (published 12 January 2021) covered 14 mother and baby homes and 4 county homes. About 9,000 children died in them between 1922 and 1998, about one in seven births and about twice the general infant mortality rate. Several homes had been linked to illegal domestic and foreign adoptions, many to the United States. On 13 January 2021 Taoiseach Micheál Martin apologised for a 'profound generational wrong'. (The care agent may hold the home-conditions record; this record focuses on removals and adoptions.)
cases.cover_up: In May 2018 Tusla referred 126 cases of births falsely registered by the St Patrick's Guild adoption agency (illegal registrations that hid children's identities).

flows.title: Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth
flows.what: The Norbertine order knew of Smyth's abuse and moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries, including assignments in the US, sometimes without warning bishops; he abused at least 143 children.

networks.name: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
networks.what: National Scout associations; the Boy Scouts of America faced more than 82,000 sexual abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy and had kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers.

networks.name: Welcome to Video
networks.what: Darknet video site paid in Bitcoin, about 1.2 million members; seized 2018. 337 arrests in 38 countries announced October 2019. Start year 2015 is not in the sources opened and is omitted from cases.

networks.name: Freedom Hosting
networks.what: Largest Tor web host in 2013, hosting Lolita City and other abuse sites; operator sentenced in the US to 27 years (2021).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Legion of Christ (Legionaries of Christ)
networks.what: Founded in Mexico in 1941 by Marcial Maciel. The Vatican said in 2010 that Maciel committed 'true crimes' and the Legion had shielded him, and placed it under a papal delegate. The Legion's December 2019 report acknowledged 175 minors abused 1941–2019, 60 by Maciel and the rest by 33 priests.

networks.name: Congregation of Christian Brothers
networks.what: Irish-founded teaching order. The Ryan Report found sexual abuse 'endemic' in its Irish industrial schools; 11 Brothers were convicted over Mount Cashel in Canada; Australia's Royal Commission found 22% of Brothers were alleged perpetrators since 1950. Its North American province filed for bankruptcy in 2011 and paid US$16.5 million to 400 victims.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2006: Kenya — Government of Kenya/UNICEF study on child sex tourism on the coast (2006).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Kenya coast — UNICEF/Government study on child sex tourism (2006)
cases.who: Tourists and local clients in Kenya's beach resorts
cases.what: On 19 December 2006 UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs launched a joint study of four beach resort areas. It found that up to 30 per cent of 12–18-year-old girls living there were involved in casual sex work and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex; 38 per cent of clients were Kenyan and 44 per cent Italian, German or Swiss tourists. Vice President Moody Awori accepted the findings and acknowledged police and community failure to enforce the law.

cases.title: Kenya — child sex trafficking in Kilifi/Kwale villas; Karamoja girls to Nairobi (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Family members, taxi drivers, recruiters; foreign and local offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report cites a 2023 NGO study estimating that more than 2,000 children were exploited in child sex trafficking in Kilifi and Kwale counties, increasingly in private villas and vacation homes rather than hotels. It also reports cross-border rings moving women and underage girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and truck drivers, miners and Lake Victoria fishermen exploiting children.
cases.cover_up: The report notes ongoing concerns of official complicity with no reported action against complicit officials.

cases.title: Kenya — babies stolen and sold in Nairobi, incl. from a government hospital (BBC Africa Eye)
cases.who: Street child-snatchers working for a buyer; illegal street clinics; a clinical social worker at a government hospital
cases.what: A year-long BBC Africa Eye investigation (November 2020) found children snatched from homeless mothers in Nairobi and sold for about £350–550, illegal street clinics selling newborns (one offered an unborn child for about £315 while paying the mother £70), and a clinical social worker at the government-run Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital who sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings (£2,000) using legitimate transfer paperwork. The reporters delivered all the children to a children's home. The BBC said the official appeared to keep his job and the clinic appeared to still operate.

cases.title: Nyumbani Children's Home, Nairobi — USAID found abuse claims credible
cases.who: Nyumbani Children's Home for HIV-positive children, run by Children Of God Relief Institute (COGRI), a Catholic charity
cases.what: Nyumbani, opened in 1992, was among Africa's first homes for HIV-positive children and attracted large US donations. After a whistleblower complaint, a 2021 USAID investigation found abuse claims 'credible', including rape of children by volunteers, caregivers and other children. The Washington Post reported the findings on 27 November 2023 from court documents filed by the orphanage's Kenyan board. The co-founder stepped down after the Post's questions.
cases.cover_up: A USAID memo (21 July 2022) said the co-founder had known of abuse allegations since 2006, 'neglected to document violence against children', permitted victim-blaming and 'systematically failed to respond to widespread sexual misconduct'; some survivors were made to write letters of apology.

flows.title: Karamoja, Uganda → Nairobi (girls for domestic servitude and sex)
flows.what: Cross-border rings ferry women and underage girls from Karamoja to Nairobi for domestic servitude or sex trafficking.

flows.title: Italy / Germany / Switzerland → Kenya coast (tourist offenders)
flows.what: The 2006 UNICEF–Government study found Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of clients of exploited children on the coast; Kenyans were 38 per cent.

flows.title: United Kingdom → Kenya (Keith Morris)
flows.what: Keith Morris was jailed for 18.5 years in the UK for 10 sexual offences against vulnerable children in Kenya, one of about eight UK prosecutions for offences abroad since 1997.

networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2022: law: Latvia law preventing adoptions to the US takes effect (1 July 2022, per US FY2024 report)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role_note: Latvia — Saeima paedophilia commission's claims against senior officials (2000), found false.
patterns.pattern_summary: False stories about child trafficking take police time and public attention away from real cases. In July 2020 a claim spread online that the furniture company Wayfair was selling children through its listings. The US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about it within days, and Polaris, the charity that runs the hotline, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed help; none of the reports contained new information. In 2016 a false claim known as "Pizzagate", that a Washington pizza restaurant was the centre of a child-abuse ring, led a man to fire a rifle inside the restaurant. In London, the Metropolitan Police spent more than £2 million on Operation Midland, which investigated claims made by Carl Beech about a ring of powerful men; the claims were false, Beech was jailed for perverting the course of justice, and he had separately admitted child sexual offences. In the 1980s the McMartin preschool case in California, built on claims of ritual abuse, cost about $14 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: Latvia — Logos Centrs child exploitation network, Riga (1999–2002 convictions)
cases.who: Logos Centrs video and model agency, Riga (director Jurijs Jurjevs)
cases.what: After a September 1999 Latvian TV report, prosecutors investigated the Riga agency Logos Centrs, headed by Jurijs Jurjevs, which The Baltic Times described as a bogus modelling agency running a child pornography and prostitution ring; seven people were charged. Andris Meinarts was convicted on 21 counts of sexually abusing minors as a customer and sentenced to ten years, the maximum; pageant agency manager Ainārs Eisaks received 2.5 years; Ingus Tūns' case was tried separately. According to Wikipedia, citing Latvijas Vēstnesis and Delfi, 67 people, 61 of them minors, were sexually exploited, the agency had catalogued about 3,000 minors, Jurjevs received more than four years and Tūns five. Claims that senior politicians were clients were investigated and found false (see the Saeima commission record).

cases.title: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
cases.who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
cases.what: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Latvia — Saeima paedophilia commission's claims against senior officials (2000), found false
cases.who: Saeima investigation commission chaired by MP Jānis Ādamsons; former PM Andris Šķēle, ex-justice minister Valdis Birkavs, State Revenue Service head Andrejs Sončiks (accused, cleared)
cases.what: After a September 1999 TV report on the Logos Centrs case, the Saeima set up an investigation commission chaired by opposition MP Jānis Ādamsons, who on 17 February 2000 publicly linked former prime minister Andris Šķēle, former justice minister Valdis Birkavs and revenue service head Andrejs Sončiks to the paedophilia case. On 1 August 2000 the Prosecutor General's Office closed the cases against them, stating it was 'fully proved' that the information given to the commission about them was false. Ādamsons was later convicted of slander; in February 2007 the Supreme Court upheld a fine of 10,400 lats. None of the officials was charged.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2004: Norway — NOU 2004:23 Barnehjem og spesialskoler under lupen.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2023: inquiry: Norway launches investigation into illegal or unethical intercountry adoptions
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State-backed adoption systems that falsified children's papers
patterns.role_note: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Norway — state investigation of illegal intercountry adoptions (2023–)
cases.who: Norwegian state; private adoption organisations
cases.what: Norway launched an investigation in 2023 into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them; the foreign ministry said it was 'aware of serious findings' (AP, 2024). Norway received 6,295 Korean children 1955–2008, and in 1974–75 Scandinavian diplomats pressed South Korea to keep sending children after it tried to stop. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee served notice of a lawsuit against the Norwegian state alleging her adoption was illegal (allegation).

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Norwegian children's homes and special schools 1945–1980 (NOU 2004:23)
cases.who: Norwegian municipal children's homes and state special schools
cases.what: The official report NOU 2004:23 'Barnehjem og spesialskoler under lupen' found neglect and abuse, in part of a serious nature and including sexual abuse, in children's homes and special schools between 1945 and 1980. Bergen and other municipalities ran their own investigations and compensation schemes; in 2005 the Storting committee recommended adapting the state 'rettferdsvederlag' scheme with payments up to NOK 300,000 and a lower burden of proof.

cases.title: Project COMPASS against 'The Com' network
cases.who: The Com (decentralised online network incl. 764, CVLT)
cases.what: Coordinated by Europol's European Counter Terrorism Centre with EU states, Norway, Switzerland, the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand (28 countries). Since January 2025 it has contributed to 30 arrests, 179 identified or partially identified perpetrators, 62 identified or partially identified victims and 4 victims safeguarded. The FBI warned the public about The Com on 23 July 2025.

cases.title: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
cases.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
cases.what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

cases.title: Thorbjørn Jagland — charged with aggravated corruption over Epstein ties
cases.who: Thorbjørn Jagland (former Norwegian PM, Council of Europe Secretary General, Nobel Committee chair)
cases.what: After the US Justice Department's 2026 release of Epstein documents, Norway's economic-crime agency Økokrim opened an investigation into former prime minister and Council of Europe secretary-general Thorbjørn Jagland on suspicion of aggravated corruption, looking into 'whether gifts, travel and loans were received in connection with his position'. On 12 Feb 2026 his lawyers said he had been charged with aggravated corruption; his Oslo home and two other properties were searched. He denies all charges. This is a corruption case, not an abuse charge; recorded for the network's political reach.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

flows.title: Seoul → Norway
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Norway; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

networks.name: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.
networks.what: RuSHA racially screened children in occupied territories and Lebensborn ran camps and homes from which selected children were placed with German families under new identities. The Nuremberg RuSHA trial (1947–48) ruled the kidnapping and Germanization of children part of genocide.

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Jeffrey Epstein and associates
networks.what: Financier Jeffrey Epstein (d. 2019) and Ghislaine Maxwell (convicted 2021) sexually abused and trafficked girls, some as young as 14, between at least 1994 and 2005 across homes in New York, Palm Beach, New Mexico, the US Virgin Islands, Paris and London. Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel was charged in France and died in custody. Banks paid hundreds of millions in settlements. 2025–2026 file releases led to misconduct and corruption inquiries against officials in the UK and Norway.

networks.what: Transnational network of online groups (incl. 764, CVLT) involved in sextortion, child sexual exploitation, swatting and other crimes; FBI public warning 23 July 2025; Europol Project COMPASS since 2025. Start year approximate.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Dominican Republic → Poland: Fr Wojciech Gil.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Fr Wojciech Gil (accused with Wesołowski) (2013): Arrested in Poland 17 Feb 2014; convicted in Poland (seven years, per NCR citation)
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: Poland — State Commission on Paedophilia, first and second reports (2021–2022)
cases.who: Polish justice system; Catholic clergy (almost 30% of perpetrators in the cases studied)
cases.what: Poland's State Commission on Paedophilia, set up by the government after a 2020 documentary on abuse and alleged cover-ups in the Catholic Church, published its first report on 29 July 2021. It analysed 345 cases and 245 court proceedings involving 188 girls and 173 boys, most aged 11 to 15. Almost 30% of perpetrators were clergy and 35% were relatives. In half the cases no one had noticed signs of abuse. The commission sent 137 notifications to prosecutors and made 22 recommendations, including ending the statute of limitations for child sexual abuse. Its second report, published on 2 August 2022, covered 513 cases; among abusers who were not relatives, clergy were the largest professional group (57 cases, about 47%).

cases.title: Poland — Diocese of Sosnowiec independent commission (2026)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Sosnowiec
cases.what: The independent commission 'Wyjaśnienie i Naprawa', set up in October 2024 and chaired by journalist Tomasz Krzyżak, presented its findings on 12 February 2026 after reviewing diocesan files from 1992 to January 2025. It found at least 50 children harmed, 96% of them under 15, and 29 people accused, 23 of them diocesan clergy; 19 of the 23 priests were confirmed offenders in church or state proceedings. Bishops were repeatedly alerted but in some cases took no action, and accused priests were often transferred rather than punished. The commission reported eight people to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Bishops were repeatedly alerted, including by reliable sources, but often took no action; where they acted, they usually moved the priest to another parish.

cases.title: Poland — bishops' 2019 figures, Sekielski films and sanctions on bishops
cases.who: Polish Episcopal Conference; Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź; Bishop Edward Janiak; Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz
cases.what: In March 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference released a study reporting 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. The Sekielski brothers' documentaries 'Tell No One' (May 2019, over 23 million YouTube views) and 'Hide and Seek' (May 2020) led to Vatican investigations of bishops under Vos estis lux mundi. In June 2020 Pope Francis put the Diocese of Kalisz under an apostolic administrator and on 17 October 2020 accepted the resignation of Bishop Edward Janiak, accused in 'Hide and Seek' of failing to act against an accused priest. Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź was also investigated, and on 6 November 2020 the Vatican imposed disciplinary measures on Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz, who died ten days later.

cases.who: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio, defunct); Ugandan lawyers and judges
cases.what: Between 2013 and 2016 the Ohio agency European Adoption Consultants arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families; families were promised their children would attend school in Kampala but they were taken to an unlicensed home. On 14 August 2020 a federal indictment charged two EAC employees and Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe (allegations; presumed innocent); an earlier employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. On 17–18 August 2020 the US State Department sanctioned Ugandan judges Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene and lawyers Mirembe and Patrick Ecobu.
cases.cover_up: Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to secure adoption orders.

cases.title: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
cases.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
cases.what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
cases.who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
cases.what: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. A church tribunal found him guilty and the Vatican announced his laicisation on 27 June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic in 2008–2013 and for possessing child abuse images, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was arrested in Poland in February 2014; on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic (2009–2013) and two in Poland.
cases.cover_up: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2024: Slovakia — bishops' commission evaluation report on abuse 2018–2023 (2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

cases.title: Slovakia — bishops' commission evaluation report on abuse 2018–2023 (2024)
cases.who: Catholic Church in Slovakia — Latin dioceses, Greek Catholic eparchies and religious orders
cases.what: The Slovak bishops' commission for the protection of minors published its 'Evaluation Report 2018–2023' in March 2024, the first such report in Slovakia, counting complaints from 1990 onward. Of 68 complaints, 39 were confirmed and closed, 17 remained open, 7 could not be resolved and 5 were not confirmed; the confirmed cases involved more than 44 victims. Fifty complaints concerned Latin-rite dioceses, three Greek Catholic eparchies and 15 religious orders.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. cases.title: Trinidad and Tobago — Sabga task force on children's homes, kept secret for 25 years
cases.who: Children's homes incl. St Dominic's Children's Home and St Jude's School for Girls
cases.what: A task force appointed by the Cabinet in 1997 and chaired by Robert Sabga visited nine children's homes. It found that a male employee at St Dominic's Children's Home had repeatedly sexually abused some 30 to 40 children and, when discovered, was asked to resign and allegedly helped to find work at a hospital; it also recorded beatings at St Jude's School for Girls. The report was never published; the Trinidad Express published its findings in May 2022.
cases.cover_up: Abuser at St Dominic's was asked to resign and allegedly helped into hospital work; report never published by government
